# Model and source

* Citation: `r readModelDb("Nakamura_2018_tamoxifen_pbpk")()$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12307> (PMC6063740, open access)
* Supplementary material used here, all from the same open-access archive:
  the Supplementary Methods (the complete ordinary differential equation
  system), Table S1 (fixed physiological and physicochemical constants),
  Table S2 (the eight Cluster Newton method parameter sets), Table S3
  (between-subject variability), Table 1 (CYP2D6 activity-based diplotype
  distribution and tumoral-ER frequencies), and the authors' deposited MATLAB
  (CNM) and R (virtual clinical study) code.

Nakamura and colleagues built a whole-body physiologically-based
pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model of tamoxifen and its four metabolites
(N-desmethyltamoxifen, 4-hydroxytamoxifen, 4-OHT-glucuronide and endoxifen),
and used it to run a prospective *virtual clinical study* (VCS): repeated
in-silico TARGET-1 trials of Japanese breast-cancer patients drawn with
realistic CYP2D6 diplotype frequencies and realistic between-subject
variability. The purpose was to predict, before the real TARGET-1 study
reported out, the probability that escalating tamoxifen from 20 to 40 mg/day in
CYP2D6-variant carriers would demonstrate superior 6-month progression-free
survival.

The whole model is packaged in one file,
`Nakamura_2018_tamoxifen_pbpk.R`: five structurally identical PBPK modules (one
per chemical species) coupled by hepatic and intestinal metabolic clearances,
88 ODE states in all. The clinical-response layer -- the stepwise endoxifen x
tumoral-ER probability model and the virtual trial -- is reproduced here as
post-processing on the simulated endoxifen concentrations, exactly as the
authors implemented it in their deposited R code, rather than as ODE states.

```{r load-model}
ui <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Nakamura_2018_tamoxifen_pbpk")())
length(ui$state) # 88 ODE states
```

# Source trace

Every model equation and every `ini()` parameter is traced to a specific
location in the paper. The parameters below are the Cluster Newton method
set ID 1 (the authors' deposited VCS worked example).

| Quantity | Source |
|---|---|
| ODE system (central, tissue, 5-unit liver, EHC chain, segregated-flow intestine, sinks) | Supplementary Methods, "Ordinary differential equations" |
| Fixed physiology (`Vliver`, `Qhep`, tissue volumes/flows, `AR`) | Table S1 |
| Fixed physicochemistry per compound (`fp`, `RB`, `Kp,*`, `fgut`) | Table S1B |
| CNM kinetic parameters per compound (`Vcentral`, `SFKp`, `ka`, `kbile`, `PSdif`, `kfeces`, `CLR`, `CLbile`) | Table S2a-e, row ID 1 |
| CNM metabolic clearances (CYP3A/CYP2D6/CYP2C9/UGT formation, "other") | Table S2a-e, row ID 1 |
| 4-OHT formation fractions by CYP2D6 / CYP2C9 (0.45 / 0.46) | Table S1B footnote; Coller 2002 |
| Between-subject variability (normal physiology, lognormal kinetics/enzymes) | Table S3 |
| CYP2D6 activity-based diplotype relative activity and %CV | Table 1 |
| Tumoral-ER expression frequencies and endoxifen response thresholds (14.3, 35.1 nM) | Table 1; Methods "Calibration of a probability model"; WHEL study |

# Population

The PK was calibrated against the mean blood concentration-time profiles of
30 healthy postmenopausal US women; the virtual TARGET-1 study simulated
Japanese breast-cancer patients. The two populations differ in body weight,
CYP2D6 diplotype frequency and tumoral-ER expression (Table 1).

```{r population}
# Table 1: CYP2D6 activity-based diplotype relative activity (reference *1/*1 = 1),
# between-subject %CV, and diplotype frequencies (%) in each population.
cyp2d6 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~diplotype,          ~activity, ~cv_pct, ~freq_white, ~freq_japanese,
  "increase/normal",   1.13,      64.3,    2.4,         1.4,
  "normal/normal",     0.89,      47.9,    43.1,        33.4,
  "normal/decrease",   0.71,      53.6,    11.2,        37.3,
  "normal/null",       0.42,      99.0,    31.8,        9.5,
  "decrease/decrease", 0.24,      66.0,    1.1,         12.5,
  "decrease/null",     0.20,      109.0,   4.3,         5.5,
  "null/null",         0.004,     103.0,   6.2,         0.5
)
knitr::kable(cyp2d6, caption = "Table 1: CYP2D6 activity-based diplotypes.")
```

# Helpers

Tamoxifen is dosed orally into the gut lumen; the absorbed fraction emerges
from the `ka` / `kfeces` competition. States are concentrations in nM and the
dose is supplied in nmol (tamoxifen base MW 371.51, so 20 mg = 53834 nmol).

```{r helpers}
MW_TAM <- 371.51
mg_to_nmol <- function(mg) mg / MW_TAM * 1e6

# Build an event table: once-daily oral tamoxifen to `days`, then an
# observation at `obs_h` (default the last trough). Observation rows use the
# first endpoint (`Cc`) so rxSolve returns every Cc* output column.
buildEvents <- function(subjects, dose_mg, days, obs_h) {
  dose_t <- seq(0, by = 24, length.out = days)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(subjects)), function(i) {
    nd <- length(dose_t)
    no <- length(obs_h)
    ev <- data.frame(
      id = subjects$id[i],
      time = c(dose_t, obs_h),
      amt = c(rep(mg_to_nmol(dose_mg), nd), rep(NA_real_, no)),
      evid = c(rep(1L, nd), rep(0L, no)),
      cmt = c(rep("gut_lumen", nd), rep("Cc", no))
    )
    ev <- ev[order(ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
    cbind(ev, subjects[rep(i, nd + no), setdiff(names(subjects), "id"), drop = FALSE])
  }))
}

# A typical subject with all enzyme activities at the wild-type reference.
typicalSubject <- function(WT = 67.58, CYP2D6 = 1, CYP3A4 = 1, CYP2C9 = 1) {
  data.frame(id = 1L, WT = WT, CYP2D6 = CYP2D6, CYP3A4 = CYP3A4, CYP2C9 = CYP2C9)
}

ssEndox <- function(cyp2d6_activity, dose_mg = 20, days = 56) {
  ev <- buildEvents(typicalSubject(CYP2D6 = cyp2d6_activity), dose_mg, days,
                    obs_h = 24 * days)
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, atol = 1e-6, rtol = 1e-6,
                       maxsteps = 1e6, returnType = "data.frame")
  s$Cc_endox[nrow(s)]
}
```

# Structural check: the CYP2D6 genotype selection criterion

The authors selected their eight parameter sets precisely because they
reproduce the reported ratio of steady-state endoxifen in CYP2D6\*10/\*10
carriers (relative activity 0.24) to that in \*1/\*1 wild-type carriers
(activity 1.0): a ratio between **0.397 and 0.472** (Supplementary Methods,
citing Lim 2007/2011 and Kiyotani 2012). Reproducing that ratio from the
packaged set ID 1 is therefore a direct, known-answer check on the whole
metabolic network and the CYP2D6 covariate action.

```{r cyp2d6-ratio}
e_wt <- ssEndox(1.00)   # *1/*1
e_dd <- ssEndox(0.24)   # *10/*10 (decrease/decrease)
e_null <- ssEndox(0.004) # null/null
ratio_dd <- e_dd / e_wt

tibble::tibble(
  genotype = c("*1/*1", "*10/*10", "null/null"),
  activity = c(1.00, 0.24, 0.004),
  endoxifen_nM = round(c(e_wt, e_dd, e_null), 2),
  ratio_to_wt = round(c(1, ratio_dd, e_null / e_wt), 3)
) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "CYP2D6 genotype" = genotype, "Relative activity" = activity,
    "Steady-state endoxifen (nM)" = endoxifen_nM, "Ratio to *1/*1" = ratio_to_wt
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Steady-state endoxifen by CYP2D6 activity (20 mg/day, typical subject).")

stopifnot(
  # The paper's selection criterion for the *10/*10 : *1/*1 endoxifen ratio.
  ratio_dd > 0.397, ratio_dd < 0.472,
  # Reduced CYP2D6 lowers endoxifen monotonically; null/null is lowest.
  e_wt > e_dd, e_dd > e_null,
  # A normal metaboliser at 20 mg/day sits in the therapeutic endoxifen band
  # (the paper's lower and upper cut-offs are 14.3 and 35.1 nM).
  e_wt > 14.3
)
```

The packaged set ID 1 reproduces the ratio (`r round(ratio_dd, 3)`), inside the
0.397-0.472 window the authors required.

# Replicating Figure 3: endoxifen across CYP2D6 diplotypes

Figure 3 shows steady-state blood endoxifen falling as CYP2D6 activity falls.
Here is the typical-value trajectory across the seven activity-based
diplotypes of Table 1.

```{r figure3, fig.height = 4}
fig3 <- cyp2d6 |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(endoxifen_nM = ssEndox(activity)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(diplotype = factor(diplotype, levels = cyp2d6$diplotype))

ggplot2::ggplot(fig3, ggplot2::aes(diplotype, endoxifen_nM)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "grey70") +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = c(14.3, 35.1), linetype = 2, colour = "steelblue") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "CYP2D6 activity-based diplotype", y = "Steady-state endoxifen (nM)",
    title = "Replicates Figure 3 of Nakamura 2018 (typical subject, 20 mg/day)",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines: 14.3 and 35.1 nM response thresholds"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

stopifnot(
  # Endoxifen is monotone decreasing in CYP2D6 activity order.
  all(diff(fig3$endoxifen_nM[order(-fig3$activity)]) <= 0)
)
```

# Single-dose pharmacokinetics and NCA

The PK was calibrated against single-oral-dose profiles (Figure S1). A
single-dose simulation of the typical subject, with PKNCA non-compartmental
analysis of the parent and the active metabolite, confirms the disposition is
well-behaved (tamoxifen and endoxifen rise and fall, endoxifen peaking much
later because it is formation-limited).

```{r single-dose}
sd_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 24, by = 1), seq(30, 168, by = 6),
                         seq(192, 672, by = 24))))
sd <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  rxode2::zeroRe(ui),
  buildEvents(typicalSubject(), dose_mg = 20, days = 1, obs_h = sd_grid),
  atol = 1e-6, rtol = 1e-6, maxsteps = 1e6, returnType = "data.frame"
)
sd <- sd[!duplicated(sd$time), ]

conc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(id = 1L, time = sd$time, conc = sd$Cc, analyte = "tamoxifen"),
  data.frame(id = 1L, time = sd$time, conc = sd$Cc_endox, analyte = "endoxifen")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(conc))

o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, conc ~ time | id / analyte)
o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(
  data.frame(id = 1L, time = 0, dose = mg_to_nmol(20)), dose ~ time | id
)
res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose))
nca <- as.data.frame(res$result)
knitr::kable(
  nca[nca$PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "half.life"),
      c("analyte", "PPTESTCD", "PPORRES")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Single-dose NCA (typical subject, 20 mg oral tamoxifen)."
)

stopifnot(
  # Endoxifen peaks later than tamoxifen (it is a downstream, formation-limited
  # metabolite), which is the qualitative signature of Figure S1.
  nca$PPORRES[nca$analyte == "endoxifen" & nca$PPTESTCD == "tmax"] >
    nca$PPORRES[nca$analyte == "tamoxifen" & nca$PPTESTCD == "tmax"]
)
```

# Virtual TARGET-1 study

One run of the virtual TARGET-1 study. CYP2D6 diplotypes are drawn at the
Japanese frequencies of Table 1; each subject's CYP2D6 activity is drawn
lognormally about its diplotype mean using the diplotype %CV (the deposited
`generatePol` routine). Variant carriers (any decreased/null allele) are
randomised to arm A (20 mg/day) or arm B (40 mg/day); wild-type/wild-type
subjects form arm C (20 mg/day). The response probability combines a stepwise
endoxifen score and a tumoral-ER score (deposited `determineProbability`:
endoxifen >=35.1 nM scores 1.0, >=14.3 scores 0.53, else 0.1; high ER scores
1.0, moderate ER 0.5; product times an adjustment factor 0.9).

The cohort here is deliberately small (the solve is 88 stiff ODEs per subject);
the paper ran 200 trials of 180 patients. The point is to show the machinery
reproduces an expected arm-B-over-arm-A superiority probability near the
paper's 0.47, not to reproduce the full 200-run distribution.

```{r vcs-population}
set.seed(20180622)
n_per_arm <- 24L

draw_cyp2d6 <- function(n, japanese = TRUE) {
  freq <- if (japanese) cyp2d6$freq_japanese else cyp2d6$freq_white
  idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(cyp2d6)), n, replace = TRUE, prob = freq / sum(freq))
  mu <- log(cyp2d6$activity[idx])
  sd <- sqrt(log((cyp2d6$cv_pct[idx] / 100)^2 + 1))
  list(activity = exp(stats::rnorm(n, mu, sd)), diplotype = cyp2d6$diplotype[idx])
}
is_variant <- function(dip) !dip %in% c("increase/normal", "normal/normal")

# Draw enough subjects to fill the variant arms A and B and the wild-type arm C.
pool <- draw_cyp2d6(3000L)
variant <- which(is_variant(pool$diplotype))
wildtype <- which(!is_variant(pool$diplotype))
armA <- variant[seq_len(n_per_arm)]
armB <- variant[n_per_arm + seq_len(n_per_arm)]
armC <- wildtype[seq_len(n_per_arm)]

mk_arm <- function(sel, dose, arm) {
  data.frame(
    id = seq_along(sel), arm = arm, dose_mg = dose,
    WT = pmax(35, stats::rnorm(length(sel), 54.44, 54.44 * 0.15)),
    CYP2D6 = pool$activity[sel], CYP3A4 = 1, CYP2C9 = 1
  )
}
arms <- list(A = mk_arm(armA, 20, "A"), B = mk_arm(armB, 40, "B"),
             C = mk_arm(armC, 20, "C"))
```

```{r vcs-simulate}
ss_days <- 56L # ~8 weeks; endoxifen is near plateau
sim_arm <- function(df) {
  df$id <- seq_len(nrow(df))
  ev <- buildEvents(df, df$dose_mg[1], ss_days, obs_h = 24 * ss_days)
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(ui), ev, atol = 1e-6, rtol = 1e-6,
                       maxsteps = 1e6, returnType = "data.frame")
  s <- s[!duplicated(s$id), ]
  df$endoxifen <- s$Cc_endox[match(df$id, s$id)]
  df
}
vcs <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(arms, sim_arm))

# Tumoral-ER status drawn at the Japanese TARGET-1 frequencies (Table 1:
# strong 0.802, moderate 0.198 among ER-positive patients).
vcs$ER <- sample(c("High", "Moderate"), nrow(vcs), replace = TRUE,
                 prob = c(0.802, 0.198))

# Deposited determineProbability().
prob_response <- function(endoxifen, ER) {
  cProb <- ifelse(endoxifen >= 35.1, 1.0, ifelse(endoxifen >= 14.3, 0.53, 0.1))
  eProb <- ifelse(ER == "High", 1.0, 0.5)
  cProb * eProb * (1 - 0.1)
}
vcs$p <- prob_response(vcs$endoxifen, vcs$ER)
```

```{r vcs-plot, fig.height = 4}
vcs$armlab <- factor(vcs$arm, levels = c("A", "B", "C"),
  labels = c("A: variant 20 mg", "B: variant 40 mg", "C: wild-type 20 mg"))
ggplot2::ggplot(vcs, ggplot2::aes(armlab, endoxifen)) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") +
  ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = c(14.3, 35.1), linetype = 2, colour = "steelblue") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Steady-state endoxifen (nM)",
    title = "Virtual TARGET-1 endoxifen by arm (one run)",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines: 14.3 and 35.1 nM response thresholds")
```

```{r vcs-outcome}
arm_mean_p <- tapply(vcs$p, vcs$arm, mean)
tibble::tibble(
  arm = c("A (variant, 20 mg)", "B (variant, 40 mg)", "C (wild-type, 20 mg)"),
  mean_response_probability = round(as.numeric(arm_mean_p[c("A", "B", "C")]), 3)
) |>
  dplyr::rename("Arm" = arm, "Mean response probability" = mean_response_probability) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Mean clinical-response probability by arm (one virtual run).")

stopifnot(
  # Dose escalation in variant carriers raises the mean response probability:
  # arm B (40 mg) above arm A (20 mg). This is the qualitative outcome the
  # paper's 200-run probability (0.469) quantifies.
  arm_mean_p[["B"]] > arm_mean_p[["A"]],
  # Escalated variant carriers (arm B) approach the wild-type standard-dose
  # arm C, the paper's equivalence comparison.
  arm_mean_p[["B"]] > 0.5 * arm_mean_p[["C"]]
)
```

A single small run cannot reproduce the paper's 0.469 point estimate (that is
the fraction of 200 runs of 180 patients in which arm B was *statistically*
superior to arm A), but the per-arm mean response probabilities move in the
reported direction: escalation raises the variant-carrier response, bringing
arm B toward the wild-type arm C.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Single-chain dispersion liver.** The Supplementary Methods and the
  deposited MATLAB code both represent the liver as five well-stirred
  sub-compartments in series (a dispersion-model approximation), each a single
  well-mixed pool -- there is no separate hepatocyte/sinusoid split and no
  active hepatic uptake transporter. The model is coded exactly that way.
* **Inter-liver transport (mass-balance reading).** The printed inter-liver
  flow term drops the partition divisor on the inflow; the deposited MATLAB
  code divides both the inflow and the outflow by `Kp,liver * SFKp`, so the
  packaged model uses the blood-equivalent concentration `Qhep * Cliver /
  (Kp,liver * SFKp)` at both ends.
* **Metabolite formation source terms (mass-balance reading).** The printed
  `Xi(t)` and `Z(t)` formation terms omit the parent's free-fraction factor
  and, in the liver, the one-fifth dispersion weight that the matching loss
  term in the parent equation carries. Both are restored so that what leaves
  the parent exactly arrives in the metabolite.
* **Tamoxifen "other" hepatic clearance.** Table S2a reports a single lumped
  `CL Other,hep` (0.966 L/h/kg); the deposited code splits it 50/50 into a
  CYP3A-dependent and a CYP3A-independent half. Because CYP3A4 is held at the
  reference activity in every simulation the paper runs, the two readings are
  numerically identical, so the packaged model carries the Table S2a lump
  without a CYP3A multiplier.
* **No residual error.** The CNM minimises a weighted sum of squares and
  reports no residual-error model, so the five `propSd` values are syntactic
  placeholders, not estimates.
* **Central-volume IIV.** The deposited parameter file carries a 30%
  lognormal between-subject variability on the central volume that is not in
  Supplementary Table S3; it is included here (shared across compounds) as the
  authors ran it.
* **Shared-process IIV names.** The between-subject random effects are applied
  once per biochemical process and shared across the five compounds (matching
  the deposited parameter file's "same"-linkage of the kinetic constants).
  Five of them (the CYP3A, UGT, "other-enzyme", intestinal-CYP3A and endoxifen
  active-efflux processes) do not correspond to a single fixed-effect
  parameter, so `checkModelConventions()` reports five IIV naming warnings;
  this is intrinsic to a coupled multi-compound PBPK, as in the
  `Toshimoto_2017_irinotecan_pbpk` sibling.
* **CYP2D6 variability.** The CYP2D6-pathway between-subject variability is
  carried by the per-subject CYP2D6 activity covariate (Table 1 diplotype
  %CV), drawn in the virtual study, rather than by a model eta.
* **Response layer in the vignette.** The stepwise endoxifen x tumoral-ER
  probability model and the virtual trial are post-processing on the simulated
  endoxifen, not ODE states (sidecar q2 option A).
* **Parameter set.** `ini()` uses CNM set ID 1 (the authors' deposited VCS
  worked example). Set ID 3 was the authors' Grubbs outlier and was dropped
  from their analyses; the other six sets can be substituted by editing the
  `ini()` block with the Table S2 values.
```
